title: A Mother's Counsel and the Woman of Valor
summary: King Lemuel records his mother's teaching: a king must not waste his strength on women or dull his judgment with wine, and he must speak up for those who cannot speak for themselves. The book then closes with an acrostic poem praising a wife of noble character, strong, industrious, generous, and wise, whose worth lies above all in her fear of the LORD.
story: Proverbs ends as it began, with wisdom embodied in a woman. The opening chapters pictured Wisdom as a woman calling in the streets and building her house (chapters 1, 8, and 9). Now, at the close, the reader meets a woman of strength who builds up her household, speaks with wisdom, and fears the LORD, the very thing the book called the beginning of knowledge in 1:7. Before that poem, the chapter gives the only section of Proverbs attributed to a woman's teaching: the counsel of a queen mother to her son. The book that opened with a father instructing his son closes with a mother doing the same.
historical:
Lemuel is otherwise unknown. His name means something like belonging to God, and no king of Israel or Judah bore it. As in 30:1, the word massa in verse 1 may mean an oracle or burden, or it may name an Arabian people, making Lemuel king of Massa. If so, Proverbs includes, and sanctifies, wisdom from outside Israel, as it does with the Egyptian material in chapters 22 to 24. Verse 2 even uses the Aramaic word bar for son rather than the usual Hebrew ben, which some take as a sign of foreign origin.

The poem of verses 10 to 31 has no author named and could have been composed at any time. Many scholars think it was placed at the end of Proverbs by the book's final editors to close the whole collection. Its picture of a household with servants, fields, vineyards, and trade in cloth fits a prosperous family in ancient Israel's towns.
cultural:
In the royal houses of the ancient Near East, the king's mother often held real influence. In Judah the queen mother (gebirah) had an official place, and the books of Kings usually name the mother of each new king. Bathsheba's role in securing Solomon's throne (1 Kings 1) shows how much weight a queen mother could carry. Lemuel's mother speaks with that authority, urging a king to protect the voiceless and to keep his judgment clear.

The woman of verses 10 to 31 works in the economy of an ancient household, where making cloth was a major part of women's labor. She selects wool and flax, spins with distaff and spindle, weaves garments and sashes, and sells them to merchants. Scarlet and purple were costly dyes, and fine linen was a luxury, so her household is well provided for. She buys a field and plants a vineyard with her earnings, which shows that women in such households could manage property and trade. Her husband sits among the elders at the city gate, where the town's affairs were settled, and her works praise her in the same gates.
literary: Verses 10 to 31 form an acrostic poem: each of its twenty-two verses begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, from aleph to taw. The form suggests completeness, praise from A to Z. The poem is full of military and heroic vocabulary. The phrase wife of noble character (eshet chayil) uses a word, chayil, often translated strength, valor, or an army. She girds herself with strength, her lamp does not go out, and the word translated food in verse 15 more often means prey. The poem has been read as a heroic hymn, a genre usually reserved for warriors, applied to a woman of everyday faithfulness. Its climax comes in verse 30, where charm and beauty are set aside for the fear of the LORD.

outline.t: Speak for those who cannot speak
The worth of a woman of valor
Her generosity, provision, dignity, and wisdom
Her praise and her fear of the LORD

doctrines.note: The poem brings the whole book to its conclusion: wisdom lived out in daily work, generosity, and speech, all rooted in the fear of the LORD (verse 30). Wisdom is not an abstraction but a life.
The chapter honors both a mother's teaching and a wife's strength. The household here is a place of work, trust, generosity, and mutual praise between husband, wife, and children.
Lemuel's mother defines a king's duty as speaking for the voiceless and defending the poor and needy (verses 8 and 9). A ruler exists to serve justice, not his appetites.

words.note: Chayil, strength, capability, wealth, or valor. It is used of warriors and armies. The phrase eshet chayil in verse 10 is often translated wife of noble character, capable wife, or woman of valor. Boaz uses the same phrase of Ruth (Ruth 3:11), and in some Hebrew manuscript traditions the book of Ruth follows Proverbs, as if presenting a real woman of valor after the poem.

Hevel, breath or vapor, the key word of Ecclesiastes. In verse 30 beauty is hevel, fleeting, like breath on a cold day. The poem doesn't despise beauty but says it doesn't last, while a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised.

Yare, one who fears. The woman who fears the LORD (verse 30) brings Proverbs back to its motto in 1:7. The fear of the LORD is reverent trust that shapes all of life, and the book ends by showing it in a person rather than stating it as a principle.

Chesed, steadfast love, kindness, or loyalty. Verse 26 says faithful instruction, literally a torah of chesed, is on her tongue. Her teaching is marked by the same loyal love that characterizes God's covenant faithfulness.

christ: Lemuel's mother describes the ideal king as one who opens his mouth for the voiceless and defends the poor. Jesus takes up that role, announcing good news to the poor and giving his life for those who had no advocate. The poem of the woman of valor also connects with the New Testament in a more thematic way. The book opened with Woman Wisdom calling people to her house, and Paul calls Christ the wisdom of God. Some Christian interpreters, following a long tradition, have also read the woman as a picture of the church, the bride of Christ, adorned with good works. That reading is allegorical and should be offered as such, but it reflects the Bible's broad pattern in which God's people are pictured as a bride and Christ as the bridegroom.

hard.q: Is the woman of Proverbs 31 a model every wife must match?
hard.a:
Readers have understood the poem in several ways. Many take it as a portrait of an ideal wife, offered to young men as a picture of what to value in a spouse (verse 10 asks who can find her) and to women as a picture of godly strength. Others read it mainly as a personification: the book began with Woman Wisdom building her house (9:1), and it ends with a woman who builds up her household, so the poem shows what wisdom looks like when embodied. Many interpreters hold both views, seeing a real woman who is the book's final portrait of wisdom lived out. In Jewish homes the poem is traditionally sung by husbands to their wives at the Sabbath meal, as praise rather than a checklist.

Whatever reading one takes, the poem is praise, not a performance standard. Its twenty-two verses present a composite picture of excellence, and it would misuse the poem to turn it into a burden that no woman can carry. Its central point is verse 30: what makes her praiseworthy is not charm, beauty, or accomplishment, but the fear of the LORD, which is open to every believer, married or single, woman or man.

questions: Lemuel's mother tells him to speak up for those who have no voice. Who around you lacks a voice, and how could you speak for them?
Verse 30 says charm is deceptive and beauty fleeting. What qualities do you praise most in others, and what does that reveal about your values?
The book of Proverbs ends not with a rule but with a portrait. Why might wisdom be best learned by seeing it lived?
